source1: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Fatimids' (dynasty 'finally overthrown by Salah al-Din (Saladin) in 567/1171') - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/fatimids
source2: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Ayyubids' (Nur al-Din's commander Shirkuh compelled caliph al-Adid to name him vizier; Saladin suppressed opposition in Egypt) - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/ayyubids
notes: Army of Zengid Syria under Shirkuh forced caliph al-Adid to appoint him vizier (1169); nephew Saladin crushed opposition and ended the caliphate 1171: external elite takeover. Q4: vizieral power struggles and Crusader invasions of the 1150s-60s.

source1: Jesmin Sultana, 'Kotalipara', Banglapedia: National Encyclopedia of Bangladesh (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh) - https://en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Kotalipara
source2: P.K. Bhattacharyya, 'Shashanka', Banglapedia: National Encyclopedia of Bangladesh (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh) - https://en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Shashanka
notes: Vanga kings (Gopachandra c.540, Dharmaditya, Samacharadeva late 6th c.) known only from copperplates centred on Kotalipara; no record of how the kingdom ended. Shashanka's Gauda later held southern deltaic Bengal; mode unknown. Dates approximate.

successor: Saadi Sultanate of Morocco (Pashalik of Timbuktu)
source1: Lansine Kaba, 'Archers, Musketeers, and Mosquitoes: The Moroccan Invasion of the Sudan and the Songhay Resistance (1591-1612)', Journal of African History 22(4), Cambridge UP, 1981 - https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-african-history/article/abs/archers-musketeers-and-mosquitoes-the-moroccan-invasion-of-the-sudan-and-the-songhay-resistance-15911612/7BE695BFE53648CF3324ED70F40512D6
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Gao' ('The Moroccans ended Songhai rule over Gao permanently in 1591') - https://www.britannica.com/place/Gao-Mali
notes: Moroccan expedition defeated Askiya Ishaq II at Tondibi (March 1591) and occupied Gao; Moroccans ended Songhai rule over Gao permanently in 1591. Askiya remnant survived in Dendi outside the core. Q4: succession war after Askiya Dawud's death (1582-88).

source1: Francois Vallat, 'Elam i. The history of Elam', Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/3, 1998 - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/elam-i/
notes: Kidinuid kings ('king of Susa and Anzan', no known kinship) followed by Igihalkids holding the same Susa-Anshan kingship; no conquest documented, transition itself unrecorded. Database 'succeeding entity' Neo-Assyrian Empire is clearly wrong. Only one accessible source.

source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tenochtitlan' ('destroyed by the Spanish conquistadores under Hernan Cortes in 1521') - https://www.britannica.com/place/Tenochtitlan
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Aztec' (Montezuma II taken prisoner by Cortes; empire came to an end in 1521) - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Aztec
notes: Spanish under Cortes (with Indigenous allies) captured and destroyed Tenochtitlan in 1521; Montezuma II died in custody, empire ended 1521. Database end 1526 too late. Q4: Texcoco succession split 1515-16 (Ixtlilxochitl vs Cacama), not verified in cited sources.

successor: Ghurid Sultanate (later Qabacha, then Delhi Sultanate)
source2: Habibullah Siddiqui, 'The Soomras of Sindh: their origin, main characteristics and rule - an overview (1025-1351 AD)', University of Karachi - https://uok.edu.pk/faculties/sindhi/docs/soomroEng.pdf
notes: Mu'izz al-Din of Ghur took Multan and Uch (1175) and compelled the Sumras of Lower Sind to accept suzerainty (1182) after reaching Debal/coast. Sumra chiefs persisted locally to 1351. Composite polity; listed capitals Thatta and Muhammad Tur postdate 1193.

source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Shunga dynasty' ('Pushyamitra assassinated Brihadratha, the last Mauryan ruler, at a military parade and assumed royal power') - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Shunga-dynasty
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mauryan Empire' (Brihadratha killed in 185 BCE by his commander in chief Pushyamitra) - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Mauryan-Empire
notes: Last Maurya Brihadratha assassinated c.185 BCE by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra, who seized power and founded the Shunga dynasty at Pataliputra: internal military coup (T0 arguable). Q4: post-Ashokan shrinkage, defections of southern princes, succession quarrels. Database -187 approximate.

source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Gortyn' (Gortyn 'shared or disputed control of the island with Knossos until the Roman annexation in 67 bce') - https://www.britannica.com/place/Gortyn
notes: No island-wide central authority; Crete was divided among poleis (Gortyn, Knossos, Lyktos etc.) that continued across 500 BCE (Gortyn disputed control with Knossos until 67 BCE). 500 BCE is a conventional period boundary. Second source inaccessible (fetch limits).

source1: Yuri Bregel, 'Bukhara iii. After the Mongol Invasion', Encyclopaedia Iranica IV/5 - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/bukhara-iii
notes: Nader Shah invaded 1740; Abu'l-Fayz Khan was defeated and submitted (vassalage). Nader's protege Muhammad Rahim (Manghit) killed the khan in 1747, ruling via Janid puppets. T2 by priority rule; otherwise internal takeover. Q4: tribal fragmentation, Kazakh ravages, famine 1720s.

source1: A. Shapur Shahbazi, 'Sasanian dynasty', Encyclopaedia Iranica, 2005 - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/sasanian-dynasty
source2: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Kawad I' ('Kawad I succeeded his uncle Walaxs (Balash) in 488, when the latter was deposed by the nobility') - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kawad-i
notes: Database split only: nobility deposed Balash and enthroned Peroz's son Kavad I (488), same Sasanian state and dynasty. Q4: Hormizd III-Peroz succession war (457-59), Peroz's defeat and death against the Hephthalites (484), drought and famine.
